entry.summary:
Decide What a Model May Draft Before It Writes: A Section Ownership Gate for Docs
A model-drafted page fails in one of two ways: it invents a fact, or it quietly overstates a promise your team cannot keep. The first failure is cheap to catch, because somebody can check a fact against a source file. The second one survives review for months, because the sentence sounds exactly like the ones your best technical writer produces. So the useful question before drafting is not "is this paragraph good?" but "was a model allowed to write this paragraph at all?". That answer depends on consequences rather than on style: a changelog entry can be wrong and fixed on Monday, while a compatibility guarantee is a promise other people plan their quarter around. entry.title: DPoP makes a token sender-constrained, which changes what a stolen token is worth
entry.summary:
DPoP makes a token sender-constrained, which changes what a stolen token is worth
Every bearer token in an OAuth deployment carries the same implicit promise: whoever holds the string can use it. That promise is what makes a leaked access token useful to an attacker and awkward for a defender. Revoking a token works, but revocation is a reaction. The better question is whether a token can be made useless to anyone who merely copies it. Demonstrating Proof of Possession, standardised as RFC 9449, is the practical answer that has reached general adoption. A bearer token is a credential in the same sense a session cookie is. If it appears in a log, a browser extension, a misconfigured proxy cache, a crash dump, or a support ticket, it is usable until it expires or is revoked. The OAuth 2.0 …

entry.title: Your Agent Patch's Green Didn't Travel: A Portability Ledger for Two-Machine Test Evidence
entry.summary: A test result is a claim about a machine, not a claim about a patch. When an agent hands you a diff plus a green suite, the suite ran somewhere. That somewhere had a Python version, a locale, a timezone, a case-sensitive filesystem, and a set of installed package versions. Change any of those and a subset of your assertions changes meaning. The patch didn't get better or worse — the evidence moved. This article is about fixing that with a small, reproducible artifact: a portability ledger. It answers one question per test — does this green survive a second machine? — and refuses to let environment drift hide behind a passing CI badge. It is deliberately not about flaky-test freezing policy, diff coverage, or mutation strength. Those are separate ledgers. This one only measures whether your…
